newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Weak, watching Japan sellers.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Weak, watching Japan sellers.

text.p: Crude prices traded in Asia swung into discount territory last week, but traders said they expected discounts to dig deeper yet.

Most traders of MidEast grades were looking to Japanese term buyers to show the first signs of aggressive discounting. With demand seen much lower for April liftings, term buyers are expected to back-out barrels onto the spot market.
"That is the only worry, if the Japanese sell it," said one major seller.
Last month, Japanese players were aggressive sellers of ADNOC grades and Oman, offering the impetus for much lower premiums.
But the Dubai differentials harldy came in at all for ADNOC grades and actually widened for Oman, providing little leeway for sellers.

At the same time Japanese and South Korean refiners enter turnarounds, refinery runs are still being cut and China's buying intentions following the Lunar New Year are still unclear, adding to the bearish sentiment.
Last week, various package deals on MidEast crudes were heard done, making it difficult to pin down a traded value for crudes.

But Murban was heard traded at a discount of four cents to ADNOC's OSP, Qatar Land swung to as much as a seven-cent discount to QGPC's OSP and Qatar Marine was heard as weak as 10 cents under, traders said.
Surprisingly for some, Oman maintained a premium status in trading, holding levels around three or four cents to MPM.
But traders said with demand seen so low in April, they expected Oman to swing into a discount as trading picks up.

Regional dealings were quiet last week with more action expected this week. There were mixed fortunes forecast, with the heavy sweet grades seen weakening but Australian production problems offering support for the light sweet grades.
Indonesia's Minas, a benchmark for heavy sweet grades in Asia, was heard traded at ICP plus 40 cents, which most traders thought was a strong premium and at the top of the expected range.
The 120,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) Dumai refinery -- which uses Minas for 70 percent of its throughput -- started a 38-day turnaround at the weekend.
And March export allocations were hardly changed at 94,300 bpd month-on-month, indicating that further allocations were expected.
"I was expecting a number more like 120,000 to 130,000," one trader said.
But traders said with so much spot Minas seen hitting the March market, premiums would drift lower in the next few weeks, possible to more like 20-40 cents.
But the light sweet market could find upward pressure on premiums amid tight Tapis availabilities and production stoppages hitting Cossack and Griffin in Australia.
Cossack loadings were delayed three to four days last week after production halved to 40,000-bpd because of a problems with gas dehydration.
A building storm then halted production at Cossack and the nearby 80,000 bpd-Griffin field. By Monday, Griffin had restarted production and Cossack was expected to restart later on Monday.
The stoppages have prompted some worries about a squeeze on liftings, especially from Griffin which has scheduled maintenance checks for the month of April.
"This could push liftings back. It will definitely affect April," one trader said. "This market is finely balanced at the best of times."
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
